strengths: Compelling motivation grounded in empirical analysis: The authors conduct a detailed error breakdown showing that 67% of multimodal RLVR failure cases stem from perception errors rather than pure logical or calculation flaws.

Methodological simplicity and elegance: PAPO modifies the core policy gradient objective by introducing an implicit perception loss (maximizing the reverse KL between original and visually corrupted inputs) combined with a double entropy regularizer. It operates as a direct drop-in replacement for GRPO/DAPO without requiring external neural reward models, teacher models, or explicit captioning supervision.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across 8 diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks with varying degrees of vision dependency using Qwen2.5-VL (3B, 7B) and Qwen3-VL (2B). PAPO achieves consistent gains (4.4% - 17.5% overall), with particularly strong improvements (up to 19.1%) on vision-dependent subsets.

In-depth analysis of training dynamics and failure modes: The paper provides a thorough examination of 'KLprcp hacking' and model collapse, clearly showing the role of the Double Entropy Loss in stabilizing training.
Strong qualitative and ablation studies: The paper provides insightful analyses on random vs. semantic masking, masking ratios, attention heatmap shifts, and error category transitions.
weaknesses: Increased computational training overhead: Computing the implicit perception loss requires an additional forward pass over rollout sequences with masked visual inputs, leading to a non-negligible increase in wall-clock time per training step (~19% on 3B and ~42% on 7B models).

Coarse token-level objective: The perception loss is applied uniformly across all tokens in the generated response, including tokens dedicated strictly to symbolic arithmetic or text formatting that do not rely on visual cues.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters: As detailed in Section 5.2 and 5.3, the model is sensitive to the weighting parameter gamma and requires careful tuning (e.g., gamma=0.04 causes collapse, and larger models are more sensitive) alongside the entropy coefficients.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: The paper identifies visual perception failure as the primary bottleneck in multimodal RLVR (accounting for ~67% of reasoning errors in GRPO) and proposes to tackle this at the objective level rather than relying on external neural reward models or heuristic pipeline stages.

Simple and effective design: Maximizing the implicit perception loss (KL divergence between policies conditioned on original vs. corrupted visual inputs) directly incentivizes the policy to generate visually grounded reasoning paths without requiring extra visual annotations.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments across multiple model scales (Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B and Qwen3-VL 2B) and eight diverse multimodal benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains, particularly on vision-dependent tasks (e.g., up to 19.1% relative improvement).

Thorough diagnosis of training dynamics and failure modes: The authors transparently analyze 'KL-hacking' / policy collapse, detailing early warning signs (divergence variance, clipping ratios, entropy spikes) and validating the proposed entropy-based regularization to ensure training stability.
Compatibility: The method is shown to be orthogonal and complementary to rollout-level enhancements such as NoisyRollout.
weaknesses: Mathematical terminology regarding entropy: In Section 3.2, the entropy regularization is defined as $H[\pi_\theta] = \log \pi_\theta(o|q, I)$, which is an empirical token log-likelihood rather than the true distribution entropy $-\sum p \log p$. While the practical motivation (preventing the policy from driving probabilities to pathological extremes) is clear, formalizing this as a log-likelihood/confidence penalty rather than entropy would avoid conceptual confusion.

Uniform application across all tokens: The implicit perception loss is applied uniformly across the entire generated token sequence, even though many intermediate reasoning steps (e.g., arithmetic derivations, generic syntax) are inherently text-based and do not directly depend on the image. A token-selective weighting mechanism is left as future work.

Additional computational overhead: PAPO requires an extra forward pass over the rolled-out response sequences conditioned on the masked image, resulting in a ~13-25% wall-clock overhead per training step.

Limited model diversity: Evaluations are conducted entirely within the Qwen-VL family (Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL). Validating on an alternative architectural paradigm (e.g., InternVL) would strengthen the universality of the conclusions.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated problem formulation: The authors provide an insightful empirical error analysis showing that visual perception failures account for approximately 67% of multimodal reasoning errors under standard RLVR (GRPO).

Principled and practical algorithm design: Rather than relying on computationally heavy auxiliary neural reward models or rigid multi-stage captioning prompts, PAPO integrates visual grounding directly into the policy optimization objective via the Implicit Perception Loss (KL divergence between original and masked visual inputs).

Thorough investigation of training stability: The paper identifies and characterizes a specific failure mode ('KL_prcp hacking' / policy collapse) and successfully introduces the Double Entropy Loss as a grounded regularization mechanism to stabilize training.

Comprehensive empirical validation: PAPO demonstrates consistent improvements across 8 benchmarks covering general and vision-dependent reasoning on multiple model sizes (Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, Qwen3-VL-2B), showing substantial gains on vision-dependent subsets and OCR tasks.
Orthogonality and modularity: The approach acts as a drop-in enhancement for both GRPO and DAPO, and demonstrates strong compatibility with rollout-level techniques such as NoisyRollout.
weaknesses: Mathematical terminology and formulation clarity: The paper formulates the entropy terms as H[\pi_\theta] = \log \pi_\theta(o|q, I), which is the realization of the sequence log-likelihood rather than the actual token-level Shannon entropy \mathbb{E}[-\log \pi]. Clarifying this distinction and formally explaining why minimizing this surrogate prevents collapse would strengthen the theoretical foundation.

Computational overhead: Computing the Implicit Perception Loss requires an additional forward pass over the full generated rollout sequence conditioned on the masked image I_mask, introducing a non-trivial increase in training wall-clock time per step (as noted in Table 14).

Hyperparameter sensitivity: The weighting factor \gamma appears somewhat sensitive to scale; larger models (7B) or settings without a reference KL penalty are prone to divergence if \gamma is slightly increased (e.g., \gamma = 0.04 causing complete collapse), requiring careful tuning of \gamma and \eta across setups.

Scope of model architectures: Evaluations are focused exclusively on the Qwen-VL family (up to 7B). Verifying transferability across diverse visual encoder architectures (e.g., InternVL) would further solidify general applicability.
